cards.explanation: The answer is that they multiply until the land is filled with them. Verse 7 says the Israelites were fruitful, increased rapidly and became exceedingly numerous, “…so that the land was filled with them.” Verse 5 counts seventy descendants of Jacob, and now the land is packed. That's a family reunion that got WAY out of hand, friends.

The answer is True. In verse 9 the king tells his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us.” Then he says, “Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more…” I think a growing crowd has him rattled, friends. That's the whole plan, and it's not a kind one.

The answer is that they will fight for Egypt's enemies and leave the country. The king says if a war breaks out, “…they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.” That's three worries stacked in one sentence, bakers. He's picturing the worst case before anything has even happened.

The word is taskmasters. Verse 11 says the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. These are the ones standing over the work and pushing, friends. It's a hard picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

The answer is Pithom and Rameses. Verse 11 says the forced labor built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. Pharaoh is the title for Egypt's king. These two cities were built by the Israelites' own hands, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 12 says, “But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished…” The pressure goes up and the numbers go up with it. The king's plan is doing the opposite of what he wanted, friends.

The answer is that they dread them. Verse 12 says the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. The Israelites keep multiplying and flourishing, and the Egyptians dread them. I think the king's plan landed him somewhere he didn't plan to be, bakers.

The word is bitter. Verse 14 says they “…made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields.” Then it adds, “Every service they imposed was harsh.” This is a heavy part of the story, friends, and the text says it plainly.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says the midwives “…did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live.” Shiphrah and Puah were told one thing and did another. That takes some serious courage, friends.

The answer is that they feared God. Verse 17 says the midwives feared God and did not do as the king had instructed. The king of Egypt gave an order, and these two women heard it and just didn't do it. The text says why: they feared God. I think that took real courage, bakers.

The answer is True. The king summons the midwives and asks, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” Then in verse 19 the midwives answer Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives.” Both parts match the text, friends.

The word is midwives. Verse 20 says God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. Shiphrah and Puah feared God, and God was good to them. It's worth noticing who the verse names, friends.

The answer is families of their own. Verse 21 says, “And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own.” Shiphrah and Puah spent their work helping Hebrew women give birth, and then God gave them families of their own. I think that's about the sweetest ending a midwife could get, bakers. I'd be hugging every one of them with my mustache.
